title: A hedge round the orchard
hookLine: defending Guru Hargobind's new ways, Bhai Gurdas says an orchard needs a thorny hedge (Bhai Gurdas, Var 26)

cards: Nobody plants a hedge of thorns for its own sake. Thorn bushes aren't pretty, and they snag your sleeve.
But walk around an old orchard, with fruit hanging low and goats wandering nearby, and the thorns suddenly make sense. They were never there for themselves. They were there for the fruit.
Bhai Gurdas reached for exactly that picture when people were troubled by a Guru who didn't look like the Gurus before him. Today: kikar.

teach.h: A GURU WITH SWORD AND HORSES.
teach.b: The Guru was Guru Hargobind. Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who took up the sword alongside the Guru's word, and kept horses and armed Sikhs around him. And some people didn't like it.

In his twenty-sixth var, Bhai Gurdas sets out what they were saying, and he doesn't soften it. The earlier Gurus sat in the dharamsal, they said, and this one doesn't stay in one place. He keeps dogs.
He goes hunting. The Gurus before him gave us hymns; this one doesn't sit and compose them.
Bhai Gurdas lets the complaints stand in full. Then he answers. The truth, he says, can't be hidden, and the Sikhs still gather round the Guru like bees round a lotus.
And then the picture that names today.
To protect an orchard, you plant a hedge of thorny kikar around it.

teach.h: THE HEDGE IS NOT THE ORCHARD.
teach.b: The hedge isn't the orchard, and it isn't the fruit.
Nobody walks into an orchard to admire the thorns. But without them, the fruit doesn't survive the season. Hear what Bhai Gurdas is claiming.
The swords and horses aren't a change of heart. The orchard is the same one Nanak planted: the Name, the sangat, the Guru's word. The hedge is what keeps it alive in hard times.
It holds together two things people tend to pull apart: gentleness and protection, a path of humility and the readiness to defend it.
Sikhs speak of this as miri and piri, the worldly and the spiritual held by the same Guru. Bhai Gurdas says it with a gardener's eye.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Hargobind for holding miri and piri together, worldly and spiritual authority, and Bhai Gurdas's twenty-sixth var is read as an early defense of that change.

o: a lotus whose blossoms draw the bees at dawn
a fruit tree whose harvest is shared in langar
a thorny tree planted as a hedge around an orchard

games.q: inside the var — tap the pairs.
p: this Guru doesn't stay in one place
the Name, the sangat, the word

s: Bhai Gurdas hides the complaints about Guru Hargobind
he sets them out in full, then answers them.
in his picture, the hedge is there to protect the orchard
the thorns aren't the fruit, but they keep it alive.

games.q: people are troubled: the new Guru keeps horses and goes hunting, unlike the Gurus before. you're Bhai Gurdas. what do you say?
o: agree the path has lost its way.
say an orchard needs a thorny hedge.
games.why: Bhai Gurdas lists the complaints in full, then says an orchard needs a hedge of thorny kikar: the hedge protects, the orchard is the same.

practice: Name one good thing growing in your life that's easy to trample: a morning routine, a friendship that's still new, a child's bedtime story, an hour that's meant to be yours.
Then ask what small hedge would keep it safe, not a wall, just a phone left in another room, a no said kindly, a time written down. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over the thing you're guarding.

wordCard.voice: Kikar, the thorny tree Bhai Gurdas pictures hedging an orchard: the orchard needs it to keep the fruit alive, answering those troubled by Guru Hargobind's new ways.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the thorny kikar tree, used for the hedge in Bhai Gurdas's picture.

carryVoice: Your line: a hedge for the orchard. The thorns were never the point; the fruit was. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 26, pauris 24–25 (complaints about Guru Hargobind; the reply, bees at the lotus, the kikar hedge round the garden)
